```{python}
V.plot(draw, size=(6.4, 3.0))
```

Steps of the three versions on their worst inputs. Doubling $n$ doubles the correct version's steps and quadruples the other two.

:::

## Pattern 6: test interactive solutions with a local judge {#sec-test-p6}

**From a fixed input to a conversation.** Every test so far fed a fixed input and read the output. In an interactive problem the judge answers your queries, so a local test needs a judge too: a small program that holds the hidden value and plays the other side.

**Recognise it.** The statement says "This is an interactive problem", describes a query format and a query limit, and asks you to flush the output.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
1. Write the solution as a function that receives `ask` (and returns the final answer), so it can run against both the real stdin/stdout and a local judge.
2. Write a judge class: it holds the hidden data, **validates** every query (range, format, distinct indices, non-empty), counts queries and fails when the limit is exceeded, and checks the final answer.
3. Run the solution against the judge for **every** hidden value when there are few, or for many random ones (including the extremes) when there are many.
4. For the real submission: flush after each query, read the answer before sending the next, exit on `-1`.
:::

**Complexity.** One judge run per hidden value; the judge's own work is usually linear in the size of the queries.

::: {#fig-test-p6}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    nodes = {
        "sol": (0, 0, "solution: ask(q)", "indigo"),
        "val": (4.4, 0, "valid query?", "violet"),
        "cnt": (8.8, 0, "count ≤ limit?", "violet"),
        "ans": (8.8, -2.2, "return answer", "green"),
        "wa1": (4.4, 2.2, "WA", "red"),
        "wa2": (8.8, 2.2, "WA", "red"),
    }
    edges = [("sol", "val", ""), ("val", "cnt", "yes"), ("cnt", "ans", "yes"), ("ans", "sol", ""),
             ("val", "wa1", "no"), ("cnt", "wa2", "no")]
    V.flow(ax, p, nodes, edges, w=3.4, h=0.8, size=10)
V.show(draw)
```

What a local judge does with each query. Invalid queries and one query too many are wrong answers, just as on the real judge.

:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-679a-bear-and-prime-100/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a fixed list of questions to adaptive ones.** Bear and Prime can ask the same fixed list of questions for every hidden number. Interview chooses each query from the previous answers (a binary search), so the local judge must also count the queries.]{.flow-bridge}


{{< include ../problems/cf-1807e-interview/problem.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** Each pattern closed one way a wrong program slips past a test: no reference to compare with, inputs without the right structure, failures too big to read, corners random inputs never reach, costs that answers do not show, and a judge that talks back. Together they make the stress loop of @sec-test-stress trustworthy.

## Pattern map

| Signal | Technique | Section |
|---|---|---|
| An unproved greedy, comparator or update rule | Stress test against brute force with a biased value pool | @sec-test-p1 |
| Bug needs duplicates or ties to show | Small value ranges, small alphabets | @sec-test-stress |
| Input is a tree, graph, DAG or set of intervals | Structured generators, several families | @sec-test-p2 |
| Counterexample found but too long to read | Shrink with chunk deletion, value shrinking, global moves | @sec-test-p3 |
| Failure in a sequence of operations | Binary search the first wrong operation | @sec-test-debugging |
| Small input space | Enumerate all small inputs | @sec-test-edge-cases |
| Many test cases per input | Multi-test generator; reset all state | @sec-test-p4-good-subarrays |
| Products, squares, sums of $10^5$ values | Max test plus an int-range checker | @sec-test-p4 |
| TLE although random tests are fast | Worst-case generators and step counting | @sec-test-p5-consecutive |
| RE on a large tree | Path generator; iterative DFS | @sec-test-p5-kefa |
| "This is an interactive problem" | Local judge with validation and a query counter | @sec-test-p6 |
| Several correct outputs | A checker, not an output comparison | exercise 8 |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **A brute force that shares the bug.** If the brute force reuses the solution's helper functions, its sort order or its boundary conventions, both agree on the wrong answer. Write it from the statement, as directly as possible.
- **A generator that cannot produce the bug.** Large value ranges, large alphabets and random-parent trees all hide whole classes of bugs. Check that the stress test catches a deliberately buggy version.
- **Invalid generated inputs.** A "tree" with a cycle, "distinct" values that repeat, $n = 0$ when $n \ge 1$. The stress test then reports bugs that the judge would never trigger.
- **Comparing outputs when many answers are correct.** Write a checker that validates the output instead.
- **Debug output on stdout.** It turns a correct answer into WA. Use stderr, and remove it before submitting TLE-sensitive code.
- **Not resetting state between test cases**: global maps, arrays, counters, flags, adjacency lists.
- **`int` for products and sums.** Check the max test; in C++ use `long long` by default for sums.
- **Recursion depth.** Python's default limit is 1000; a path of $10^5$ vertices crashes a recursive DFS.
- **Forgetting to flush** in interactive problems: Idleness limit exceeded.
- **Floating-point equality.** Compare floats with a tolerance (absolute or relative $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-9}$), both in the checker and in the code.
- **Trusting "no counterexample found".** It is evidence, not proof: a generator can only find what it can produce.
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E]** A stress test with arrays of length 1 to 8 and values in $[1, 10^9]$ passes 10 000 tests, but the solution gets WA. Give two likely reasons.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(1) The bug needs equal values (duplicates, ties), and with values up to $10^9$ random arrays almost never repeat a value: shrink the range to 1..5. (2) The bug only appears at larger sizes or extreme values: overflow, recursion depth, a per-test reset, or a case the generator never produces (empty input, $n$ exactly 1 when the generator starts at 2). Also check that the brute force is not wrong in the same way.
:::

**2. [E] (coding)** Write a generator for a random **permutation** of $1..n$ and one for a random array of $n$ **distinct** values from $[lo, hi]$. Check that their outputs are valid.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`random.shuffle` on `list(range(1, n + 1))` and `random.sample(range(lo, hi + 1), n)`. `random.sample` does not build the range list, so it is fast even for a huge range.

```{python}
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(0, 20)
    p = rand_perm(n)
    assert sorted(p) == list(range(1, n + 1))
    d = rand_distinct(n, -5, 30)
    assert len(set(d)) == n and all(-5 <= x <= 30 for x in d)
```
:::

**3. [E] (coding)** This function returns the second largest **distinct** value, or `None`. Find its bug by an exhaustive sweep and fix it.

```python
def second_largest(a):
    first = second = 0
    for x in a:
        if x > first: first, second = x, first
        elif x > second and x != first: second = x
    return second if second != first else None
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Initialising with 0 invents a value that may not be in the array. The exhaustive sweep, in order of length, finds the smallest failure at once: on `[1]` it returns 0 instead of `None`; on `[-1, -2]` it returns 0 instead of $-2$. Start from `None` (or $-\infty$) and treat "no value yet" explicitly.

```{python}
def second_largest_buggy(a):
    first = second = 0
    for x in a:
        if x > first:
            first, second = x, first
        elif x > second and x != first:
            second = x
    return second if second != first else None

def second_largest(a):
    first = second = None
    for x in a:
        if first is None or x > first:
            first, second = x, first
        elif x != first and (second is None or x > second):
            second = x
    return second

def second_brute(a):
    d = sorted(set(a))
    return d[-2] if len(d) >= 2 else None

bad = next(a for a in all_arrays(4, [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]) if second_largest_buggy(a) != second_brute(a))
print("smallest failing input:", bad)
assert bad == [1]
assert all(second_largest(a) == second_brute(a) for a in all_arrays(5, [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]))
```
:::

**4. [M] (coding)** Check that Prüfer decoding gives each of the $5^3 = 125$ labelled trees on 5 vertices exactly once when it is run on all $125$ sequences (Cayley's formula).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Decoding is a bijection between sequences in $\{1..n\}^{n-2}$ and labelled trees, so running it on every sequence must give 125 distinct trees, each a valid tree. This is also why a uniformly random sequence gives a uniformly random tree.

```{python}
trees = [frozenset(frozenset(e) for e in prufer_to_tree(list(seq), 5)) for seq in product(range(1, 6), repeat=3)]
assert len(trees) == 125 and len(set(trees)) == 125
assert all(is_tree(5, [tuple(e) for e in t]) for t in trees)
```
:::

**5. [M] (coding)** Write a generator for a random **connected** graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges that may contain self-loops and multi-edges (some problems allow them). Check connectivity with BFS.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Start from a random spanning tree (guarantees connectivity) and add $m - n + 1$ edges with endpoints chosen independently, allowing $u = v$ and repeats.

```{python}
def rand_multigraph(n, m):
    edges = rand_tree_parent(n)
    edges += [(random.randint(1, n), random.randint(1, n)) for _ in range(m - (n - 1))]
    random.shuffle(edges)
    return edges

def connected(n, edges):
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    seen, q = {1}, deque([1])
    while q:
        v = q.popleft()
        for w in adj[v]:
            if w not in seen:
                seen.add(w)
                q.append(w)
    return len(seen) == n

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 12)
    m = random.randint(n - 1, 3 * n)
    g = rand_multigraph(n, m)
    assert len(g) == m and connected(n, g)
```
:::

**6. [E]** Your C++ solution passes locally and gets "Runtime error on test 5". The input has $n \le 10^6$ and you declared `int a[100000];` globally. What happened, and which flag would have caught it locally?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The array is ten times too small: writing `a[i]` for $i \ge 10^5$ is out of bounds. Sometimes this crashes (RE), sometimes it silently overwrites other globals (WA). `-fsanitize=address` reports the out-of-bounds write with a line number; `vector` with `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` also checks `operator[]`. Read the constraints again and size arrays from them (plus a small margin).
:::

**7. [M]** Explain why a solution to a problem with $t \le 10^4$ test cases and $\sum n \le 2\cdot10^5$ that calls `memset(cnt, 0, sizeof cnt)` on a global `int cnt[1000001]` at the start of each test gets TLE, and give two fixes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each `memset` writes 4 MB; $10^4$ tests write 40 GB, about $10^{10}$ bytes, far over the time limit, although the "real" work is only $2\cdot10^5$. Fixes: (1) after each test, reset only the entries you touched (loop over the test's values and set `cnt[v] = 0`); (2) use a timestamp array: store `when[v] = test_id` and treat `cnt[v]` as 0 when `when[v] != test_id`. A per-test `map` or `unordered_map` also works.
:::

**8. [M] (coding)** For a problem with many correct outputs (any topological order of a DAG), write a **checker** and stress-test Kahn's algorithm with it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The checker validates the output against the input: it must be a permutation of the vertices, and every edge must go forward. It never compares with another solution's output.

```{python}
def kahn(n, edges):
    indeg, adj = [0] * (n + 1), defaultdict(list)
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        indeg[v] += 1
    q = deque(v for v in range(1, n + 1) if indeg[v] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        v = q.popleft()
        order.append(v)
        for w in adj[v]:
            indeg[w] -= 1
            if indeg[w] == 0:
                q.append(w)
    return order

def check_topo(n, edges, order):
    if sorted(order) != list(range(1, n + 1)):
        return False
    pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(order)}
    return all(pos[u] < pos[v] for u, v in edges)

for _ in range(500):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    edges = rand_dag(n, random.randint(0, n * (n - 1) // 2))
    assert check_topo(n, edges, kahn(n, edges))
assert not check_topo(3, [(1, 2), (2, 3)], [2, 1, 3])
```
:::

**9. [M]** In C++, why can `sort` with the comparator `[](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }` crash, and how do you detect it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`std::sort` requires a **strict** weak ordering: `comp(a, a)` must be false. With `<=`, `comp(a, a)` is true, and the unguarded inner loops of introsort can run past the end of the range when many elements are equal: undefined behaviour, often a crash or corrupted data. `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` checks the comparator and aborts with a message; `-fsanitize=address` catches the out-of-bounds read. Use `<`.
:::

**10. [M] (coding)** Check by brute force that the concatenation comparator "$x$ before $y$ iff $x + y > y + x$" (which arranges numbers into the largest number) is a strict weak ordering on all digit strings of length 1 to 3 over the digits 0–2, and that the comparator "$x$ before $y$ iff $x + y \ge y + x$" is not.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Test irreflexivity (`not before(x, x)`) and transitivity (`before(x, y) and before(y, z)` implies `before(x, z)`) over all triples. The non-strict version fails irreflexivity at once.

```{python}
strs = ["".join(p) for k in (1, 2, 3) for p in product("012", repeat=k)]
before = lambda x, y: x + y > y + x
before_ge = lambda x, y: x + y >= y + x
assert all(not before(x, x) for x in strs)
assert all(before(x, z) for x in strs for y in strs for z in strs if before(x, y) and before(y, z))
assert any(before_ge(x, x) for x in strs)
```
:::

**11. [M]** What is the risk of `x * y % MOD` in C++ when `x` and `y` are `int` values below $10^9 + 7$? And when they are `long long` values below $10^{18}$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With `int` operands the product is computed in `int` and overflows (it can reach $10^{18}$); cast first: `1LL * x * y % MOD`. With `long long` operands up to $10^{18}$, the product can reach $10^{36}$, beyond 64 bits; use `__int128` (`(__int128)x * y % m`) or a multiplication-by-doubling routine. The edge sweep should include $x = y = m - 1$.
:::

**12. [M] (coding)** Shrink a failing **multi-test** input for the reset bug of @sec-test-p4-good-subarrays to the smallest one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The case is a list of test strings. Shrink by deleting tests, then shortening and lowering each test's digits. The result has two one-digit tests: the second sees the first one's counter.

```{python}
def smaller_tests(case):
    (tests,) = case
    def smaller_test(s):
        if len(s) > 1:
            yield s[1:]
            yield s[:-1]
        for i, ch in enumerate(s):
            if ch != "0":
                yield s[:i] + str(int(ch) - 1) + s[i + 1:]
    for c in smaller_list(tests, lambda s: list(smaller_test(s))):
        if c:
            yield (c,)

fails_reset = lambda c: not_reset(make_input(c[0])) != good_brute(make_input(c[0]))
random.seed(4)                                    # derive each test from a seed: the shrunk answer must be reproducible
start = ([rand_string(8, "0123") for _ in range(6)],)
assert fails_reset(start)
minimal = shrink(start, fails_reset, smaller_tests)[0]
print("minimal failing tests:", minimal)
assert len(minimal) == 2 and all(len(s) == 1 for s in minimal)
```
:::

**13. [H]** In a contest you have a WA on test 47 of a problem with a single test per input, you cannot see the test, and your stress test passes. List what you would try, in order.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(1) Reread the statement and constraints against the code (indexing, inclusive bounds, special output such as $-1$). (2) Edge sweep: $n = 1$, extremes, all equal, max values — especially **overflow**, since stress tests use small values. (3) Strengthen the generator: larger $n$ (with a faster brute force, e.g. $O(n^2)$ instead of $O(n!)$), larger value ranges, other structures (paths, stars, duplicate-heavy arrays). (4) Write a second, independent fast solution and stress the two against each other on large inputs. (5) Compile with sanitizers and `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` and run the large random tests: undefined behaviour can pass small tests by luck. (6) Check output format for big answers (scientific notation for floats, precision).
:::

**14. [H] (coding)** Write an **adaptive** judge for "guess $h \in [1, n]$; each query $q$ is answered `lower`, `higher` or `equal`": it keeps the set of values consistent with all answers so far and always answers so as to keep the larger part. Show that binary search needs exactly $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ queries against it, and that querying $lo + 1$ (a "lazy" search) needs $n$ queries in the worst case.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The adversary keeps an interval $[lo, hi]$ of candidates. For a query $q$ in it, the parts below and above $q$ have sizes $q - lo$ and $hi - q$; it answers so that the larger part survives, and says `equal` only when both are empty. Against binary search on an interval of size $s \ge 2$, the surviving part has size $\lfloor s/2 \rfloor$, so the number of queries is $f(s) = 1 + f(\lfloor s/2 \rfloor)$ with $f(1) = 1$, which is $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$. This matches the decision-tree lower bound of @sec-pf-lower-bounds. The lazy search always queries the bottom of the interval, so the adversary removes one value per query.

```{python}
class AdaptiveGuessJudge:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.lo, self.hi, self.queries = 1, n, 0
    def ask(self, q):
        self.queries += 1
        below, above = q - self.lo, self.hi - q
        if below <= 0 and above <= 0:
            return "equal"
        if above >= below:
            self.lo = q + 1
            return "higher"
        self.hi = q - 1
        return "lower"

def binary_guess(n, ask):
    lo, hi = 1, n
    while True:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        r = ask(mid)
        if r == "equal":
            return mid
        lo, hi = (mid + 1, hi) if r == "higher" else (lo, mid - 1)

def lazy_guess(n, ask):
    lo = 1
    while True:
        r = ask(lo)
        if r == "equal":
            return lo
        lo += 1

for n in range(1, 300):
    j = AdaptiveGuessJudge(n)
    binary_guess(n, j.ask)
    assert j.queries == n.bit_length()               # floor(log2 n) + 1
    j = AdaptiveGuessJudge(n)
    lazy_guess(n, j.ask)
    assert j.queries == n
```
:::

**15. [H] (coding)** Two programs compute the mean of a list of floats in different orders and print it with 9 decimals. Show that comparing outputs exactly gives false alarms, and write a checker with absolute or relative error $10^{-6}$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Floating-point addition is not associative, so the last digits can differ. Judges accept an answer when $|x - y| \le \varepsilon \max(1, |y|)$; the checker must do the same.

```{python}
def mean_forward(a):
    return sum(a) / len(a)

def mean_backward(a):
    s = 0.0
    for x in reversed(a):
        s += x
    return s / len(a)

def close(x, y, eps=1e-6):
    return abs(x - y) <= eps * max(1.0, abs(y))

exact_mismatch = 0
for _ in range(500):
    a = [random.uniform(-1e6, 1e6) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 50))]
    x, y = mean_forward(a), mean_backward(a)
    exact_mismatch += f"{x:.9f}" != f"{y:.9f}"
    assert close(x, y)
print("exact comparison would report", exact_mismatch, "false failures out of 500")
assert exact_mismatch > 0
```
:::

**16. [H]** Codeforces "hacks" can make `unordered_map<long long, int>` take $\Theta(n^2)$ time. Why, and how do you defend against it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For integers, libstdc++ uses the identity hash, and the bucket count follows a known sequence of primes. A hacker can choose keys that are all multiples of the bucket count, so they all land in one bucket and each operation scans a chain of length up to $n$. Defence: a hash with a random, per-run seed, for example splitmix64 applied to `x + FIXED_RANDOM`, where `FIXED_RANDOM` comes from `chrono::steady_clock::now()`. Alternatives: `map` ($O(\log n)$ guaranteed), or sorting and coordinate compression. Locally, test with keys $k \cdot P$ for the bucket-count prime $P$ to see the slowdown.

```cpp
struct SplitMix {
    static uint64_t f(uint64_t x) {
        x += 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15; x = (x ^ (x >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9;
        x = (x ^ (x >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111eb; return x ^ (x >> 31);
    }
    size_t operator()(uint64_t x) const {
        static const uint64_t R = chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count();
        return f(x + R);
    }
};
unordered_map<long long, int, SplitMix> cnt;
```
:::

**17. [E]** Your program prints the right answers locally but gets "Wrong answer on test 1". The sample input has two test cases. Name three causes that have nothing to do with the algorithm.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(1) Debug output left on stdout. (2) Output format: missing newline between answers, `Yes` instead of `YES`, extra spaces where the checker is strict, too few decimals. (3) State not reset: the second test case of the sample sees the first one's data — locally you may have tested each case separately. Also: reading input in the wrong order, or a local file redirection (`freopen`) left in the code.
:::

## Interview questions

**1. How would you test the function you just wrote?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Walk through the edge cases out loud (empty, one element, two elements, all equal, negatives, the maximum size and overflow, boundaries), trace one small normal case by hand, and say that in practice you would compare it against a brute force on many small random inputs. Mention the specific risky line ("the `<=` in the loop condition") and test it.
:::

**2. What is a stress test, and why are its inputs small?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Run the optimised solution and a slow, obviously correct brute force on thousands of random inputs, and stop at the first difference. Inputs are small so that the brute force is fast, so that a failing case is easy to read, and so that small value ranges produce the duplicates and ties where bugs hide. Almost all bugs that exist for large inputs also exist for some small one.
:::

**3. Your solution passes the samples but you are not sure it is correct. You have 10 minutes left. What do you do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a brute force (five lines: all subsets or permutations), a generator with $n \le 8$ and values in 0..5, and a compare loop. Run it for a minute. If it finds a counterexample, shrink it by hand or by deleting elements, and fix. If not, check the edge cases and overflow on the max test, then submit.
:::

**4. Your solution gets TLE. How do you find out why?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
First compare the intended complexity with the budget from the constraints. Then generate worst-case inputs (max $n$; sorted; all equal; a path graph; many duplicates; many tiny test cases) and time them locally, doubling $n$ to see the growth rate. Look for hidden costs: `x in list`, `list.pop(0)`, string concatenation in a loop, copying vectors by value, clearing a big array per test, slow I/O (`cin` without `sync_with_stdio(false)`, Python `input()` instead of `sys.stdin`), and hash tables under adversarial keys.
:::

**5. A recursive DFS crashes on large inputs in Python. What are your options?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The default recursion limit is 1000 and the interpreter's C stack is limited too. Options: convert to an explicit stack (iterative DFS, or process vertices in BFS order and then in reverse order for bottom-up computations); or raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` and run the code in a `threading.Thread` after `threading.stack_size(...)` to get a bigger stack. The iterative version is the robust choice.
:::

**6. How do you test a function whose output is not unique, for example "return any valid topological order"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a checker that validates the output against the input (a permutation of the vertices; every edge goes forward), instead of comparing with a reference output. For optimisation problems with many optimal solutions, the checker verifies the solution is valid and that its value equals the brute force's optimal value.
:::

**7. What is shrinking, and why does it help?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Repeatedly replacing a failing input with a smaller one that still fails (delete parts, make values smaller) until no smaller variant fails. The minimal input typically has two or three elements and isolates the cause: "two equal values", "one interval inside another", "two elements when $lo = mid$". It is what property-based testing tools (QuickCheck, Hypothesis) do automatically; the systematic version is Zeller's delta debugging.
:::

**8. How do you generate a random tree? Is it uniform?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Simplest: for $i = 2..n$ connect $i$ to a random earlier vertex, then shuffle the labels. That is not uniform over labelled trees, and its height is only $O(\log n)$ on average. For uniform trees, decode a random Prüfer sequence of length $n - 2$ (there are $n^{n-2}$ sequences and as many labelled trees). For testing, add paths, stars and caterpillars explicitly, since they are the extreme cases for depth and degree.
:::

**9. On Codeforces your solution passes test 1 but fails on test 2, which has many test cases. What is the most likely bug?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
State carried between test cases: a global counter, map, visited array, adjacency list or answer variable that is not reset. Or an early `return`/`break` that leaves part of a test's input unread, so the next test reads garbage. Fix by putting per-test state inside the test loop and reading the whole input of each test even when the answer is known early.
:::

**10. What is "Idleness limit exceeded" and how do you avoid it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In an interactive problem, both programs are waiting: usually your query is still in the output buffer, so the judge never receives it. Flush after every query (`endl`, `fflush(stdout)`, `print(..., flush=True)`). It also happens when you read input the judge never sends (wrong protocol), or when you forget to print the final answer.
:::

**11. How do you test an interactive solution locally?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a local judge: it holds the hidden data, validates each query, answers it, counts queries against the limit, and checks the final answer. Structure the solution so that it takes an `ask` function, and run it against the judge for all hidden values (or many random ones and the extremes). To test the real binary, run the judge as a separate process connected through a pipe. An adaptive judge (adversary) checks the worst case of the query count.
:::

**12. How do you detect and prevent integer overflow?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Estimate the largest intermediate value from the constraints (max $n$ × max value, products, squares, $n(n+1)/2$ counts). Use 64-bit types for anything that can exceed about $2\cdot10^9$, cast before multiplying (`1LL * a * b`), compare as `a > LIMIT / b` instead of `a * b > LIMIT`, and use `__int128` for products of 64-bit values. Detect it with `-fsanitize=undefined` (signed overflow) and with a max-value test. In Python, wrap results in a range check to simulate C++ types.
:::

**13. Should asserts stay in submitted code?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cheap asserts that check assumptions (an index range, "this case cannot happen") can stay: a failing assert gives RE instead of a silent WA, which tells you something. Expensive checks (re-verifying an invariant over the whole array each iteration) must go, or be guarded by a debug flag, because they change the complexity. In Python, `python -O` removes asserts, so never put side effects inside them.
:::

**14. What do `-fsanitize=address,undefined` and `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` catch?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
AddressSanitizer: out-of-bounds reads and writes on heap, stack and global arrays, use-after-free, double free. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: signed integer overflow, invalid shifts, division by zero, misaligned or null pointer use. `_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`: bounds checks on `vector::operator[]`, invalid iterator use, and comparators that are not strict weak orderings in `std::sort`. All slow the program down, so use them on the failing test, not to measure speed.
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Stress test:** brute force (from the statement) + solution + generator (tiny $n$, tiny values) + compare loop; a crash is a failure.
- **Generators:** `sample` for distinct, `shuffle` for permutations, small alphabets for strings, random parent / Prüfer / path / star for trees, tree + extra edges for connected graphs, forward edges in a random order for DAGs; one seed per test.
- **Shrink:** delete chunks, delete items, shrink values, global moves; stop when no smaller candidate fails.
- **Edge sweep:** empty, 1, 2, all equal, sorted, extremes, overflow at max size, multi-test with several cases, enumerate all small inputs.
- **Verdicts:** WA → stress + edges + overflow; WA on test 2 → reset; TLE → worst-case generators and step counts; RE → bounds, recursion depth, division by zero; ILE → flush.
- **Interactive:** solution takes `ask`; local judge validates, counts, checks; test every hidden value.
:::

- The generator decides which bugs you can find: bias it towards duplicates, ties, prefixes, zeros and extreme shapes.
- Check that your stress test catches a deliberately buggy version; otherwise you do not know it tests anything.
- A brute force must be written independently of the solution, directly from the statement.
- Shrunk counterexamples explain bugs; long random ones only prove they exist.
- Random inputs are average cases; TLE and RE need deliberate worst cases.
- Many "wrong ideas" are right ideas with overflow, a missing reset or an off-by-one at a boundary.
- In C++, compile with warnings always and with sanitizers when hunting.
- For interactive problems, the local judge is the stress test, and flushing is not optional.

## Further reading

- **Kernighan and Pike**, *[The Practice of Programming](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/295125)*, ch. 5 (debugging) and ch. 6 (testing): boundary testing, test scaffolds, and how to narrow down a bug.
- **Zeller**, *[Why Programs Fail](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/why-programs-fail/9780123745156/)*: delta debugging and the systematic simplification of failing inputs.
- **Claessen and Hughes**, *["QuickCheck: a lightweight tool for random testing of Haskell programs"](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/351240.351266)* (ICFP 2000): property-based testing with generators and shrinking; the Python library **[Hypothesis](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/)** follows the same ideas.
- **CP-Algorithms**, *[Prüfer code](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/pruefer_code.html)*: the bijection between sequences and labelled trees, and an $O(n)$ decoder.
- **GCC documentation**: [sanitiser options](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Instrumentation-Options.html) (`-fsanitize=address`, `-fsanitize=undefined`) and the [libstdc++ debug mode](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/debug_mode_using.html) (`_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`).
